records.title: Scotland Against Spin
records.bodyText:
Herald letters
In his support of Rosebank, Grant
Aitchison (Letters, October 28) makes a simple but telling point which so far hasn’t received the emphasis it deserves in the oil debate.
Which is that oil has a myriad of different uses other than simply the generation of energy, on which oil deniers focus.
For the overall picture, ask Google: “What are the uses of oil?” I did, and the AI answer was a long list of products, following the general comment that crude oil (petroleum) is primarily used to produce transportational fuels,
generate energy and manufacture over 6,000 everyday products, including plastics, synthetic fibres and chemicals.
Are oil deniers ignorant of all this? Or do they believe that if we buy our oil needs from other extracting countries, rather than extracting it ourselves, this will somehow polish our net zero credentials?
Whatever the case, oil deniers cannot be allowed to avoid discussing a future without oil, without identifying the substitutes, if any, that they believe could be used instead to maintain the supply of all the products we have currently, courtesy of oil.
Alan Fitzpatrick, Dunlop, Ayrshire.

MT FOX RESIDENTS RALLY TO PROTECT WILDLIFE
Residents, wildlife carers and environmental advocates have gathered at Mt Fox to voice concerns about the proposed Gawara Baya wind farm, raising questions about habitat clearing, increased traffic, noise and impacts on vulnerable wildlife.
Located just 4.8km from the Wet Tropics World Heritage Area, the project has prompted community concern, while developer Windlab says biodiversity protection and ecological restoration are key priorities. 
Read more here: https://shorturl.at/O3FtY
#HinchinbrookLife #Local #Community #Support #MtFoxRally

records.title: Environmentalists Against Wind Turbines
records.bodyText:
Is This the End for Hope Moor Wind Farm? 
Plans for 23 wind turbines, each over 200 metres tall, on moorland between Arkengarthdale and Teesdale have hit a major obstacle.
The Ministry of Defence (MOD) has objected, warning that the proposed development could cause unacceptable interference with RAF air defence and air traffic control radars, as well as obstruct low-flying military aircraft.
Developer Fred. Olsen Renewables says it is working with the MOD, other stakeholders and the local community to explore practical solutions.
Will the project overcome these concerns, or could this be the beginning of the end for Hope Moor Wind Farm?
#HopeMoor #WindFarm #YorkshireDales #RenewableEnergy

records.bodyText:
Scottish & Southern Electricity Networks (SSEN) has confirmed a greenfield site near Muir of Pert just over 4km north-east of Brechin, as its preferred site being taken forward for its proposed new 275kv Substation.
SSEN's announcement follows local consultations with communities and stakeholders across Angus and Aberdeenshire held in May 2026.
SSSEN says the development will be known as the Muir of Pert 275kV substation. SSEN has published its report on its consultation that had identified Site 2 at Pert and an alternative Site 16 at former Edzell airfield.
Read the Report on Consultation https://www.ssen-transmission.co.uk/.../report-on...
SSEN's Lead Community Liaison Manager Louise Anderson says "The report summarises the feedback received on Site 2 and the alternative Site 16 near RAF Edzell. It also explains how we considered this feedback alongside environmental, technical and economic assessments.
"We consulted between May and July 2026, holding public events in Edzell, Stacathro, Craigo and Brechin. We would like to thank everyone who attended an event or provided feedback.
"We will now progress the project into the pre-application and concept design stage, supported by further surveys and environmental assessment.
"We plan to hold a further round of public consultation in February 2027 and will provide more information nearer the time."
When SSEN announced its consultation for the proposed new substation it's brochure explained that the new East Coast 275Kv Substation and Connections Project is required to enable a new connection location of the upgraded Bridge of Dun GSP substation and to enable the removal of over 82km of existing 132Kv Overhead Lines throughout Aberdeenshire & Angus.
However, the newly announced report on the May 2026 recent community Consultations now states as follows: "The project is required to support future renewable generation connections and support reinforcement of the East Coast transmission network" Begs a question: Which future connections? Ossian Wndfarm? Glenskinno Solar?
SSEN also published its East Coast Future Transmission Projects brochure file https://www.ssen-transmission.co.uk/.../muir-of-pert.../

records.title: Scottish Electricity Generating Stations
records.bodyText:
Vattenfall has completed all 14 turbine foundations at its 63MW Clashindarroch II Wind Farm in Aberdeenshire, a major construction milestone delivered in 11 weeks. 
The foundations used 11,256m³ of lower-carbon concrete and approximately 1,190 tonnes of recycled reinforcing steel — equivalent to the weight of 826 cars. Reusing steel reduces demand for newly produced material. 
The concrete contains a cement blend with at least 25% pulverised fuel ash, replacing part of the conventional Portland cement. As Portland cement is the most carbon-intensive component, the blend is expected to reduce embodied carbon by around 20–30% per cubic metre. Concrete was produced at a temporary on-site batching facility, reducing long-distance deliveries and the associated fuel use, traffic movements and emissions. 
The first foundation was poured on 30 June 2026. Around 85 tonnes of reinforcing steel was used in each foundation. Construction will now move to the next phase, with first power expected in summer 2027. 
Once operational, the 14-turbine wind farm is expected to have an installed capacity of 63MW3 and generate enough renewable electricity to power the equivalent of around 61,500 UK homes annually. 
Jones Bros Civil Engineering UK has been contracted by Vattenfall to deliver roads and access tracks, electrical infrastructure, turbine foundations and other infrastructure as part of the construction of Clashindarroch II Windfarm.
The company will upgrade nine miles of existing and five miles of new access tracks, construct 14 turbine foundations and associated crane hardstanding, and undertake cabling work to connect the site to Cairnford substation.
Jones Bros and Vattenfall have worked together to provide an in-depth social value commitment plan, which factors in jobs, skills and workforce development, the supply chain, and community.
The project package will create over 120 jobs at the site during construction, and a minimum of two new apprentice opportunities will be created. One paid work placement for an engineering undergraduate at a local college or university is also on offer.
Key Project & Delivery Details
• Project Capacity & Turbines: 14 Vestas V136 (4.5 MW each) onshore wind turbines.
• Turbine Manufacturer: Vestas Wind Systems AS.
• Tower Innovation: Features lower-carbon steel towers (using 100% scrap melted via wind-powered electric arc furnace from ArcelorMittal in Industeel Charleroi, Belgium), reducing tower carbon footprints by 36%.
• Civil & Balance of Plant: Jones Bros Civil Engineering UK is managing site infrastructure, upgrading 9 miles of existing tracks and building 5 miles of new routes to accommodate heavy and abnormal-load component deliverie
Powersystems will be responsible for delivering the critical electrical infrastructure required to connect the wind farm safely and efficiently to the electricity network. Working within the Scottish DNO network area, Powersystems will undertake the design, supply, installation, testing and commissioning of the project’s 33 kV electrical connection infrastructure.
The scope of works includes:
• Supply, installation and testing of the 33 kV cable connection and fibre optic communications network between the Cairnford 275/33 kV Substation and the Clashindarroch II Wind Farm substation.
• Installation of approximately 33 kV underground cable circuits along the wind farm access route, including cable jointing, terminations and network testing.
•Supply and installation of a 24-fibre single-mode armoured fibre optic cable and associated communications infrastructure.
Supply, installation and commissioning of the shared 33 kV switchboard serving both Vattenfall Renewables and Vattenfall iDNO operations.
• Installation of a 110V DC battery charger system to support switchgear control, protection and tripping functions.
• Supply and installation of power quality and disturbance recording equipment.
Installation of a COP2 metering panel and emergency trip facilities.
•Completion of all associated commissioning, VLF cable testing and OTDR fibre optic testing activities.
Clashindarroch II wind farm will provide around £315,000 per annum in community benefit funding to the local community .— at Clashindarroch.

records.bodyText:
Are Offshore Wind Farms Delaying Coast Guard Rescues?
https://newenglandboating.com/are-offshore-wind-farms.../
A prominent commercial fishing industry advocate is raising the alarm that New England’s rapidly expanding offshore wind farms are actively delaying life-saving U.S. Coast Guard rescues at sea. Speaking on 77 WABC with John Catsimatidis, Bonnie Brady, policy director of the New England Fishermen’s Stewardship Association, (NEFSA), stated bluntly that offshore turbines are compromising maritime safety, pointing to three recent examples.
Her first concern stems from a recent medical evacuation near an offshore wind construction site. According to Brady, a Coast Guard broadcast on emergency Channel 16 explicitly stated help would arrive in 10 minutes “if it can make way past the wind farms.” Flight tracking data later showed an MH-60 helicopter taking a critical 12 minutes just to descend near a turbine. In a story covering the accident, the Mass Daily News noted they could not independently confirm the radio transmission.
Brady’s second example involves the tragic October 3rd crash of a Latitude Air Ambulance jet south of Nantucket. In this case, Brady argues the turbines severely hampered the recovery. She claims a Coast Guard fast response cutter was forced to detour around the grid, adding 30 minutes to its transit.
The most haunting example ties into a seven-year-old maritime mystery. The fishing vessel Mistress sank off Block Island on New Year’s Day 2019, claiming two lives. This September, the advocacy group Green Oceans announced it located the missing wreckage—along with apparent human remains—sitting 92 feet down and just 50 feet from a Block Island Wind Farm turbine. Green Oceans president Michael Lombardi suggests the hull’s position indicates “the captain may have made a fatal starboard maneuver to avoid the turbine.”
Written by Tom Schlichter

records.bodyText:
Loch Doon dam was intially built to create a head of water for the hydro-electric power station required to power the target system and other elements of the Loch Doon Gunnery School. 
In initial dam was constructed at Loch Doon in 1916, as part of the attempt to create an Aerial Gunnery School nearby.
The purpose of the dam was to raise the level of the loch by 6 ft, to provide sufficient head of water to drive a hydroelectric generating scheme to power the school and its systems.
Loch Doon Aerial Gunnery School was located to the west of Dalmellington, on the site of a World War I airfield constructed for the purpose between the B741 road and Bogton Loch. The airfield was part of a disastrous attempt by the War Office to establish a gunnery school on site, which began in 1916, and ended unsuccessfully two years later, having consumed at least £500,000 to no useful end. The true cost was never disclosed, and various accounts of the school raise this figure to £1 million, while others climb to £3 million. 
Regardless of the correct figure, correcting any of the figures given to express the cost in current monetary terms means this would be reported by the media as a multi million pound Government funded scandal.
Conceived by Colonel (later Brigadier General) Sefton Brancker when he discovered a similar facility some 35 miles from Bordeaux, while active service in France, the school was an inspired concept in a world where the military saw aircraft as a novelty, good only for observation and token gestures such as hand-thrown bombs with little real destructive effect. 
Having achieved the position of Deputy Director of Military Aeronautics before resigning his post and serving abroad, Brancker was able to use his prior position to win acceptance of the concept. The scheme called for a landlocked body of water, and on paper at least, Loch Doon met this requirement, and was also well positioned close to steeply sloping hills, which would provide a suitable location on which to site the tracks for the target bogies.
The airfield was probably the outstanding folly established on the site, and appears to have been created without any consideration for local knowledge which could have been provided by the area's residents. The completed airfield was found to virtually useless, rendered largely inoperable by the combined effects of the marshy land it had been built on, and the adverse weather conditions which affected the location was all but useless for the aircraft types that were supposed to operate and train from the field.
The gunnery ranges were located in the nearby hills, and comprised rail mounted targets which zigzagged up and down the hillsides, followed by the trainee gunners, also on tracks, in carriages with guns mounted to reproduce their installations in aircraft.
Construction of the school had been a massive undertaking, requiring the construction of a light railway to the south west of Dalmellingto facilitate the work. Completed around April 1917, the track ran from a point about 200 metres northwest of Dalmellington Station, to the Airfield, and terminated in the area of Dalfarson, less than a mile to the south. A plan to extend the railway to the north end of Bogton Loch which would have involved blasting for a new tunnel, finally resulted in the Air Ministry examining the whole plan and ultimately led to the project being questioned and halted.
In addition to the airfield and railway, the plan also called for the construction of a dam and hydroelectric scheme on Loch Doon; an accommodation camp for 500 men in 18 brick built barracks; further accommodation for 1,500 civilian contractors working for Messrs McAlpine (the contractor) and for some 1,200 German PoWs employed as labourers. The site was also provided with a 400 seat cinema, sewage treatment works and water supply system. The airfield was equipped with workshop, stores, and had two centrally heated hangar Intended to cater for both land and sea planes, purpose built seaplane hangars were located to the south, on the west shore of Loch 
Nothing significant remains of the airfield, and RAF aerial photographic surveys carried out after World War II showed the area had already been cleared of the installation. The seaplane hangars are also known to have been lost when construction of a local reservoir flooded the area. The school's own dam raised the level six feet, and the later works in 1936 raised this another 30 feet, engulfing the hangars which were necessarily located at the water's edge. Trace evidence of the gunnery school can still be found in the area, with some sections of the zigzag ranges and trenches still extant, and visible on the ground.
The later Loch Doon Dam provides the main seasonal storage for the upper three power stations on the Dee. Its original level was raised 27 ft by the construction of the dam across its natural outlet at the northern end.
The total length of the dam is 980 ft, the main central portion consisting of a mass concrete structure of the gravity type, slightly curved in plan. There is a 16 ft wide roadway along the crest. Flood water is dealt with by the 110 ft wide spillway assisted by a group of three siphons on the north flank. An interesting feature of the dam is the fish pass, which rises spirally inside a circular concrete tower within the reservoir.
This dam was also completed in 1937. The consulting engineer was Sir Alexander Gibb & Partners and the main contractor, Sir Robert McAlpine & Sons Ltd.
This latter dam drowned the elements of the gunnery school which were located close to the waters edge and raised the water level to form a major element of stage two of the Galloway Hydro-electric Scheme. It supplied water to the Water of Deugh, and hence to power stations at Kendoon, Carsfad, Earlstoun.
and Tongland.
Loch Doon Dam (1936)
Purpose: seasonal storage
Type: gravity
Maximum height of footway above river-bed: 43ft (13.1m)
Total length along crest: 980ft (298.7m)
Spillway level: 705ft (22.9m) OD
Normal maximum depth over crest: 3ft (0.9m)
Overfall spillway length: 110ft (33.5m)
Syphons (3): 5ft 6ins (1.7m) outlet diameter
Normal maximum spillway capacity: 4675 cusecs
This dam controls the outflow from Loch Doon allowing storage capacity to be developed in the loch. Water is fed out at the South end of the loch into the River Deuch which conveys it down towards Kendoon. The dam is at the North end of the loch and regulates the flow across the watershed of the River Doon. The dam has a highly unusual octagonal section spiral fish ladder integrated into the upstream wall. This dam is of combined arch and gravity type and has an integrated spillway. The arcaded parapeted walkway to the top accommodates the public road. The design contains a highly unusual fish ladder which consists of an octagonal drum with an ascending spiral of linked water filled chambers. The dam is a significant landscape feature in an area of low moorland terrain.
This dam was intended solely to control the level of the loch, and so has neither integral nor directly associated generating capacity.
Drumjohn Hydro Power Station was added 1984 on the culvert / pipework between Loch Doon outlet and the Water of Deugh.— at Loch Doon.
